title: Family and home
goal: Talk about your family and where you live — while picking up the whole set of Malaysian household words.
bekal: name family members with the right Malaysian words
describe a house and its rooms
use *ada* and *dengan* to talk about having things and being together

notes: **Adik-beradik** = siblings, brothers and sisters. It comes up in every family introduction. *Berapa orang adik-beradik?* = "How many brothers and sisters do you have?" (literally, "how many siblings [are you] in all?").

**Abang** means **older brother** — and also a friendly way to address any man a bit older than you. An older sister is **kakak**, or **kak long / kak ngah** (eldest / middle daughter). For younger siblings Malay has just one word, **adik**, for both boys and girls.
**Kecik** is the spoken form of *kecil* (small), and you'll hear it everywhere. In writing it's always *kecil*.

**Jangan segan-segan** = don't be shy, make yourself at home. **Segan** means **shy, reluctant out of politeness**. *Saya segan nak tanya* = I feel awkward asking. (⚠️ Indonesian *segan* leans towards "unwilling".)
**Sunyi** = quiet, lonely. **Bising** = noisy. Both are the standard everyday words in Malaysia.

grammars.title: Saying what belongs to whom
body: The owner goes **after** the thing, with no linking word — like "the house of me" without the "of". *Rumah saya* = my house.

English
Note
rows: Spoken: *Yang mana punya awak?* (Which one is yours?)

after: For "have", Malay uses **ada** (there is): *Saya ada dua abang* = I have two older brothers. *Awak ada kereta tak?* = Do you have a car?
*Dengan* = with: *saya pergi dengan Aina* (I'm going with Aina). In speech it's often shortened to *ngan* or replaced with *sekali* (together): *saya pergi ngan dia*, *saya pergi dia sekali*.

blocks.text: Two that often trip learners up: **ibu bapa** (parents — one idea, not two separate people) and **anak saudara** (nephew or niece — not "a relative's child" in general). Both appear on forms and in everyday talk.

⚠️ **Datuk** has two very different meanings: at home it means **grandfather**, but in front of a name it's an **honorary title** awarded by a sultan or the state — *Datuk Seri*, *Datuk*. Calling an elderly man "Datuk" is fine, but addressing a title-holder by his bare name is considered impolite.

blocks.title: Asking about family
items: **Berapa orang adik-beradik?** — How many brothers and sisters do you have?
**Awak anak yang keberapa?** — Where are you in the family? (first, second…?)
**Ibu bapa awak kat mana?** — Where are your parents?
**Dah berkahwin ke belum?** — Are you married yet? (a very ordinary question in Malaysia)
**Ada anak tak?** — Do you have children?
⚠️ Questions about marriage, age and salary are far more normal in Malaysia than in many Western countries. They aren't nosy; they're how people get to know you.

blocks.text: This table is long on purpose: this is the vocabulary that leaves learners speechless in a Malaysian home even when they've mastered the grammar. Six to learn first: **tingkap** (window), **katil** (bed), **tilam** (mattress), **peti sejuk** (fridge, "cold box"), **kerusi** (chair) and **ubat gigi** (toothpaste — literally "tooth medicine"). Notice the English loans: *siling*, *garaj*, *sinki*, *suis*, *paip*.

Types of housing in Malaysia have their own names, which you'll see in rental ads: **rumah teres** (terraced house), **rumah berkembar** (semi-detached house), **banglo** (bungalow, detached house), **pangsapuri** (apartment ⚠️), **kondominium**, **rumah flat** (low-cost flats), **rumah kampung** (traditional house on stilts). For renting: **sewa** (rent), **deposit**, **tuan rumah** (landlord), **penyewa** (tenant).

blocks.title: Visiting a Malaysian home
items: **Assalamualaikum** at the door — and wait for a reply before going in.
**Tanggalkan kasut** (take off your shoes) before going in. This isn't optional; almost every home in Malaysia expects it.
**Jangan segan-segan.** — You'll hear this. It means: make yourself at home.
**Dah makan?** — Not small talk. If you say you haven't, food will appear.
**Sedap!** — Praise the food. This matters and is expected.
**Terima kasih jemput saya.** — Thank you for inviting me. (⚠️ *jemput* = invite)
